# Reproducing and Stress-Testing Two Approaches to LLM Reasoning Reliability: Test-Time Probability Aggregation and Logic-Representation Editing

- **Authors**: Minhan Cho, Jimin Kweon
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-09
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08514>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08514v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-interpretability
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-interpretability 0.50, test-time-scaling 0.25

## In one line

Independently reproduces two published reliability methods and stress-tests them across models and domains their authors never tried, finding one reproduces exactly but loses significance everywhere new, and the other rests on a decodable logic direction that a same-norm random direction matches exactly under steering.

## Problem

Two recent methods attack reasoning reliability from opposite ends of the stack -- one aggregating token probabilities with self-consistency at inference, the other training projectors that split hidden states into content and logic and editing the logic part toward a valid region. Both were evaluated only by their own authors, neither was independently reproduced, neither was stress-tested across models or domains, and one shipped no public code. Validating such claims matters because reliability is precisely the property that has to hold outside the conditions it was demonstrated in.

## Contributions

- An independent reproduction of two reliability methods that were evaluated only by their own authors, with one of them having shipped no public code, extended to models and domains the originals never covered.
- The demonstration that an inference-time aggregation method reproduces its published numbers exactly while failing to reach significance against plain self-consistency on any new domain or public benchmark, with per-item paired tests rather than averages.
- A direct test of the original authors' own explanation for a negative result -- insufficient sampling budget -- confirming its direction while showing the resulting advantage rests on 2 of 80 items and vanishes when the evaluation set is enlarged.
- A mechanistic precondition for probability-aggregation methods: uncertainty and answer diversity are necessary but not sufficient, because the path probabilities must also carry information about which answer is correct.
- A decomposition of the representation-editing method showing that its assumed logic-validity direction is real at one sub-layer (probe accuracy 0.82) and at chance across the layers the method edits (0.52), against a semantic control at 0.95 everywhere -- so representation editing works for semantic attributes and logic validity is encoded weakly and locally.
- The null control the original lacked: a random direction of the same norm swept over the same strengths traces the same curve as the supervised direction, establishing that the probe-validated direction buys no controllability over noise.
- A mechanical diagnosis of why a conditional steering gate is inert -- it fires on 98 percent of tokens because reference and task activations come from different distributions -- and a matched-distribution redesign producing the study's only positive steering result, by ablating a content direction rather than adding a validity one.
- An explicit, non-accusatory account of a headline that cannot be reproduced because it depends on an unreleased component.

## Method

Both methods are reimplemented and first checked against their original settings, then extended along the axes their papers did not cover: the aggregation method to four constructed domains and three public benchmarks with a single backbone, and the representation-editing method to four models of 7 to 8 billion parameters. Statistical discipline is applied uniformly and is the study's backbone -- per-item paired Wilcoxon tests rather than comparisons of averages, bootstrap intervals over items, multiple seeds for both sampling and projector retraining, and explicit reporting of how many individual items separate two methods. The sampling-budget hypothesis offered by the original authors for a negative result is tested directly by generating more paths and re-aggregating at growing budget. For the editing method the study goes past reproduction into diagnosis: a held-out linear probe measures whether a logic-validity direction exists and at which layers, with a semantic attribute on a separate corpus as a positive control; the additive intervention is swept over strengths with a norm-relative shift; the trained projector is decoded at the single best sub-layer; and a random direction of the same norm is swept over the same range as a null. A training-free alternative from the steering literature is then implemented faithfully, including a k-nearest-neighbour conditional gate with automatic layer selection, and finally a controlled syllogism task crossing formal validity with believability is built so that reference and task activations come from the same distribution.

## Results

The aggregation method reproduces its original grid almost exactly, matching the published accuracy and calibration figures to two decimal places. Extended, it never significantly beats plain self-consistency anywhere: across four new domains no per-item difference reaches significance (paired Wilcoxon p at least 0.28 on every one), and across three public benchmarks it ties on one, edges another by 1.1 and trails a third by 2.0, again with nothing significant. One domain is diagnostic rather than merely null -- the model is uncertain and answer-diverse, the two preconditions the method needs, and it still only ties -- which yields the study's clearest mechanistic statement: uncertainty and answer diversity are necessary but not sufficient, because the path probabilities must additionally carry information about which answer is right, and on that task they do not. The budget hypothesis is then tested and half-vindicated in a way worth recording. Scaling from 8 to 32 sampled paths moves the method from below self-consistency to a 2.5-point lead that nearly halves calibration error, so the direction is as its authors predicted -- but at the larger budget only 2 of 80 items separate the two methods, the paired test does not reach significance, the bootstrap interval on the gap is [0.0, +6.3], and enlarging the evaluation set to 200 items erases the advantage entirely, turning it into -0.25 at p = 0.85. The editing method fares worse. Its headline effect rises on one of four models but not significantly (p = 0.56), and the same recipe significantly degrades two others (p below 0.001 and 0.002) and reduces the effect on a fourth; on a public logic benchmark it degrades even the one model it helped. Retraining the projector under five seeds shows that lone gain is stable across training rather than a single-run artifact, which the authors report in its favour, while noting it remains item-concentrated and per-item non-significant. The diagnosis is the valuable part. A held-out probe separates valid from invalid conclusions at 0.82 accuracy at the single best sub-layer -- so the direction the method assumes does exist -- but collapses to 0.52, chance, when pooled over the layer range the method actually edits, while the same probe on a semantic attribute reaches 0.95 across all layers. Steering along that direction then buys nothing: the additive intervention gives no consistent gain over a strength sweep, decoding the trained projector at the probe's peak layer leaves the effect unchanged on both models (p = 0.90 and 0.40), and a random direction of the same norm traces the same curve as the supervised one over the same strength range. So separability and controllability come apart -- the direction is decodable and is not a causal lever. The training-free alternative fails for a mechanically identifiable reason: its conditional gate fires on 98 percent of tokens and therefore behaves as static steering, because a classifier 0.88-separable on short reference sentences classifies nearly every task token as steer-worthy when reference and task come from different distributions. Removing that mismatch with a matched-distribution syllogism task produces the study's only positive steering result, and it is narrow in three ways the authors enumerate: it requires the matched distribution, it works by ablating the believability direction rather than by adding the validity one, and it only helps a model that already performs the task, since the other answers a constant no at chance. Their conclusion is that model capability rather than the intervention is the dominant factor.

## Limitations

Stated and acted on. Evaluation sets are small and the authors repeatedly decline to claim effects their own tests do not support, including for the method they are most sympathetic to -- the 2.5-point budget-scaling lead is reported as at most a weak directional signal, and its disappearance on a larger set is put in the results rather than buried. One constructed corpus is flagged as a contiguous block rather than a random sample with citation-derived noisy labels; a benchmark's label parse rate of 74 percent is reported; one model's reimplementation is marked as not on the same scale as the others because it was run on different hardware and library versions, with only the direction of its effect treated as comparable. On the unreproducible headline the phrasing is exact and worth quoting: the original's most dramatic number relies on a discriminator that was not released, the authors' analogue is degenerate in that it marks every generation valid for one model, an auditable third-party judge shows no gain, and they state they find no evidence of fabrication but that the headline leans on an unauditable component and so cannot be reproduced as stated. Not stated but worth noticing: the study is one backbone for the aggregation method and four 7-8B models for the editing method, so 'model-dependent' is established over a narrow capability band, and several of the constructed domains are the authors' own.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-interpretability**: This is the strongest single instance in the archive of detection and control coming apart, and it is strong because of the control the original paper omitted. A held-out probe finds a logic-validity direction at 0.82 accuracy, which by the usual standard would license the whole intervention -- and then a random direction of the same norm, swept over the same strengths, traces the same behavioural curve as the supervised one. Not a weaker effect: the same curve. Decoding the trained projector at exactly the layer where the probe peaks leaves the target metric unchanged on both models (p = 0.90 and 0.40). The authors' phrasing is the one to carry: separability and controllability come apart, and a decodable direction is not a causal lever. Two further diagnoses generalise beyond this method. The probe's layer profile explains why the recipe fails rather than merely showing that it does -- 0.82 at the single best sub-layer, 0.52 at chance pooled over the layers actually edited, against a semantic attribute at 0.95 everywhere. So logic validity is encoded weakly and locally while semantic attributes are encoded strongly and globally, which predicts that representation editing transfers to the second kind and not the first, and gives a concrete reason to check a direction's layer profile before choosing where to intervene. And the conditional-gate failure is a mechanically identified distribution mismatch: a gate 0.88-separable on short reference sentences fires on 98 percent of task tokens, degenerating to static steering, because the references and the task come from different distributions. Any gated or conditional intervention in the archive should be checked for its firing rate, which is a one-line diagnostic that distinguishes a working gate from an inert one. The one positive steering result is instructive in what it required: a task where reference and steering distributions match, ablation of the content direction rather than addition of the validity direction, and a model that could already do the task -- with the authors concluding that model capability rather than the intervention is the dominant factor. Finally, the study is a model of how to report an irreproducible result: the original's headline depends on an unreleased discriminator, the authors' analogue is degenerate, an auditable judge shows no gain, and they state they find no evidence of fabrication but that the number leans on an unauditable component and cannot be reproduced as stated. That is the register such a finding should be written in. One further half of the study bears on this topic's neighbour and is worth recording here since it travelled under the same protocol: the inference-time aggregation method reproduces its published numbers to two decimal places on the original setting and then fails to significantly beat plain self-consistency on any of four new domains or three public benchmarks. Its precondition analysis is the transferable part -- uncertainty and answer diversity are necessary but not sufficient for confidence-weighted aggregation to beat majority voting, because the path probabilities must additionally carry information about which answer is correct, and one tested domain satisfies both preconditions while the confidence carries nothing. And the budget-scaling episode is the sharpest methodological lesson: the original authors attributed a negative result to insufficient sampling budget, the reproduction tests that directly, confirms the direction, and then reports that at the larger budget only 2 of 80 items separate the methods, the bootstrap interval on the 2.5-point gap starts at 0.0, and enlarging the evaluation set to 200 items turns the gap into -0.25 at p = 0.85. A scaling curve can move in exactly the predicted direction and still be nothing.

## Abstract

We independently reproduce two recent methods for making large language model (LLM) reasoning more reliable, and stress-test them across domains and models (RPC across four new task domains with Qwen3-8B, LCF across four 7-8B models). The first, RPC, aggregates token probabilities and self-consistency at inference; the second, LCF, trains projectors that split hidden states into "content" and "logic" and edits the logic part toward a valid region. Validating such reliability claims matters because the original evaluations are run by each method's own authors and were never independently reproduced or stress-tested across models and domains, and LCF shipped no public code. We re-run RPC's published-path aggregation and re-implement LCF's projector, contrastive, and intervention pipeline, then extend both to text-to-SQL, legal extraction, fallacy identification, and precedent grading, and probe LCF's representation directly. RPC reproduces the original grid exactly on the authors' released reasoning paths; on four new domains its edge over self-consistency is never significant (ties or small mixed differences, paired p >= 0.28), and on BIRD, the one domain where we vary the budget, the edge grows with K as predicted but its largest gap (+2.5 accuracy at K=32, p=0.16) reverses to -0.25 when we enlarge the sample to n=200. LCF's logic-validity direction is real but weak (0.82 separability at the single best sub-layer versus 0.95 for a semantic-attribute control); its one positive effect (Qwen3 $Δ$Prob) is not significant (p=0.56), while it significantly reduces $Δ$Prob on two of the other three models.
